name: Parser Differential
summary: A situation where two components parse the same input in different ways. An attacker can use the gap so that one component checks one thing and the other executes another.
explanation:
Many systems process the same message more than once. A proxy reads a request, then the server reads it. A verifier checks a file, then an installer opens it. A filter inspects an address, then a mail server delivers to it. A parser differential exists when those components don't interpret the input in exactly the same way. The first one approves what it sees. The second one acts on something else.

**Examples**:

- **HTTP request smuggling**: A front-end proxy and a back-end server disagree about where a request ends, for instance when `Content-Length` and `Transfer-Encoding` are both present. The attacker hides a second request inside the first one
- **Certificate names with null bytes**: A certificate authority read the full name, `www.bank.com\0.attacker.com`, and saw a domain owned by the attacker. Some browsers stopped at the null byte and saw `www.bank.com`
- **Android "Master Key"**: An app package with two entries of the same name. The signature check read one. The installer used the other
- **Duplicate JSON keys**: One parser keeps the first value, another keeps the last. A check on one side and the action on the other see different data
- **URL parsing**: An allowlist check and the HTTP client extract different hosts from the same odd URL. It's a common path to server-side request forgery

**Why it happens**:

- Specifications are ambiguous or incomplete, so each implementer fills the gaps differently
- Parsers are lenient, and each one recovers from malformed input in its own way. That's the dark side of Postel's Law
- Formats are complex: several ways to express a length, nesting, optional encodings
- The same input goes through different libraries and languages

**Defenses**:

- **Parse once**: Parse at the boundary and pass the parsed result on, not the raw bytes (see Parse, Don't Validate)
- **Reject ambiguity**: Duplicate keys, conflicting lengths or invalid encodings are errors. Don't pick a winner
- **Use the same parser** for the check and for the use, when that's possible
- **Re-serialize**: Forward a normalized form of the message instead of the original
- **Prefer simple formats** with one possible interpretation (see Language-Theoretic Security)
- **Differential fuzzing**: Send the same inputs to both parsers and compare the results
